findings.reason: the worker must know whether the new kind blocks and must be given `reckon/hooks/coordinator_obligations.py` to change it, or it lands a row that re-creates the reported symptom under a new name.
findings.text: §105 adds the `scope-held` kind but adds it to neither `NON_BLOCKING_DUTY_KINDS` (`reckon/crew/obligations.py:187-190`) nor the hook's mirror `_NON_BLOCKING_KINDS` (`reckon/hooks/coordinator_obligations.py:240-242`), and the hook blocks every kind outside that set (`:1513`), so a scope-held row holds every stop open on a claim only the holding run's landing releases — the same undischargeable-duty defect the section exists to remove; the hook module is also absent from the write paths.

findings.reason: the mechanism needs a field added at the recorder (and that file in scope), otherwise the node must parse provenance out of a refusal's prose, which the module's own docstring warns against.
findings.text: §105's third rule compares a `session_refusal`'s age against the pointer's hold verdict, but the refusal is a `dict[str, str]` written by `_queued_failure_remedy` (`reckon/crew/recovery_classification.py:220-260, 1317, 2449-2468`) carrying only `detail` and `next_command` — no recorded instant, no holding run and no path — so "older than an open hold verdict" and "naming the holding run and the path" cannot be read from it as the deliverable assumes, and that writer is outside §105's write paths.

findings.reason: a worker landing on the cited range reads a different duty's construction and can change the wrong block.
findings.text: §105 cites `reckon/crew/obligations.py` "near lines 1880–1893" for the row built from the queued pointer's `session_refusal`, but 1880–1893 is the `plan-review-owed` append; the cited branch is `if row.get("session_refusal")` at 1906–1909.

findings.reason: the named write path covers a file the station has never written, so the node would either extend the station to a new path the read order in `obligation_snapshot.py:279/469/518` may not consult first, or fix a file the hook still reads stale.
findings.text: §109 has the station rewrite "that session's exported snapshot", naming `crew/obligations/power_convertor/13a7ba33….json`, but that path is `obligation_snapshot.snapshot_path(project, session)` written by the producer (`reckon/crew/obligation_snapshot.py:240-242, 1164`); the station writes only `station_snapshot_path(project)` — one project-wide file whose `sessions` map is built from `store.obligation_rows()`, after `_drop_absent` has deleted the dropped session's row (`reckon/crew/station_obligations.py:205-219, 277-315`).

findings.reason: a case that passes on the defect proves nothing about the "not repeated while absent" half of the deliverable, so the node can land a rewrite that fires every tick and still be green.
findings.text: §109's second case, "a second publish with the session still absent leaves the file's mtime unchanged", holds on the unfixed code: inside `EXPORT_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS` `export_snapshot` returns before writing anything regardless of the fix (`reckon/crew/station_obligations.py:259-265`), so the case cannot fail and its guard is unmeasured; the only negative control covers the first case.

findings.reason: an exclusive write scope must be determined before dispatch, and a node choosing the module itself may write one a concurrent node holds, which is the failure the fleet rules fence against.
findings.text: §110 writes "the follower module the manifest names for the settle rule", leaving the module that decides settling unnamed even though it is identified elsewhere in the plan as `reckon/crew_follow_commands.py` (`FOLLOWER_SETTLE_EVENT` at :371, `_settle_grace_default` at :398); the nearby §107 names that file explicitly.
